sm: Georgia Howe talks with Penny Nance, CEO and president of Concerned Women for America, about a new teen trend called looks maxing, in which kids go to extreme lengths to look better than their peers. Nance says it is part of a push by teens to get drugs without their parents knowing. The drug in question is retatrutide, a next-generation weight loss drug from Eli Lilly that is still in FDA study and has no legal version for sale. Bootleg versions are being sold through social media and even convenience stores, and Nance says some come from the same companies that made fentanyl precursors. She notes that CBS reported at least two deaths, that kids as young as 13 are being coached by peers on hiding needles, and that nobody knows if the products hold fentanyl, other contaminants or bacteria. She also worries about stunted growth and about missing emergency room reporting.

Howe asks why the companies are still operating, and Nance answers that China allows it and that shipments arrive illegally, sometimes labeled as research, with a large bust in Cincinnati. She says kids get it more like buying from a convenience store than from a street dealer, using code names and misspellings to evade social media takedowns, and that the two deaths were adult women. On regulation, she understands the real drug could reach the market legally in about a year. She says she supports GLP-1 drugs for adults, citing family members who benefited, but wants them legal, safe and under a doctor's care. She compares looks maxing to heroin chic and the eating disorders of the 80s and 90s. Her advice to parents is to open a conversation, ask what their kids and their friends know, listen to image struggles, and see a doctor when needed.
